content: Chandani Anoma Jayathilaka, representing the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia, contributed to this work. Cheryl Johnson, from the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and STIs Programmes, also provided her expertise. Rita Kabra, Edward Talbott Kelley (formerly of the Department of Integrated Health Services), and Rajat Khosla (formerly of the Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health, SRH) were key contributors. James Kiarie, from the Department of SRH, and Hyo Jeong Kim, from the Department of Health Emergency Interventions, also played significant roles. Loulou Kobeissi and Antonella Lavelanet, both from the Department of SRH, provided their expertise, as did Arno Muller and Carmem Pessoa Da Silva from the Department of Surveillance, Prevention, and Control. Michaela Pfeiffer, from the Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Health, and Marina Plesons, from the Department of SRH, also contributed. Vladimir Poznyak, from the Department of Mental Health and Substance Use, and Michelle Rodolph, from the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and STIs Programmes, were involved as well. Ritu Sadana, from the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health and Ageing, and Diah Saminarsih, from the Office of the Director-General, provided their input. Anita Sands, from the Department of Regulation and Prequalification, and Lale Say, from the Department of SRH, also contributed. Elisa Scolaro, from the Department of Health and Multilateral Partnerships, and Olive Sentumbwe-Mugisa, from the WHO Country Office in Uganda, were key participants. Agnes Soucat, from the Department of Health Systems Governance and Financing, and Anna Thorson and Igor Toskin, both from the Department of SRH, also provided their expertise. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, from the Department of Health Emergency Interventions, and Isabelle Wachsmuth, from the Department of Integrated Health Services, contributed as well. Tana Wuliji, from the Health Workforce Department, and Souleymane Zan, from the WHO Country Office in Cotonou, Benin, were involved. Qi Zhang, from the Department of Integrated Health Services, also participated. Additionally, WHO consultants Michalina Drejza (formerly of the Department of SRH), Carmen Figueroa (from the Department of Global Tuberculosis Programme), and Megha Rathi (from the Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Health) provided their expertise. Special thanks are extended to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee, particularly its Secretariat members Susan Norris and Rebekah Thomas Bosco, for their invaluable feedback throughout the guideline development process. Writing support for the WHO was provided by Briana Lucido. Administrative support was offered by Jane Werunga-Ndanareh and Michael Tabiszewski. Communications support was provided by Catherine Hamill, Sarah Kessler, Christine Meynent, and Elizabeth Noble, all from the WHO Department of SRH. Editing and proofreading services were provided by Green Ink, based in the United Kingdom. The overall coordination of the guideline development process was led by Manjulaa Narasimhan from the WHO Department of SRH. Funding for the development of the guideline was provided by the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development, and Research Training in Human Reproduction, as well as the Children’s Investment Fund Foundation. The WHO guideline on self-care interventions for health and well-being, revised in 2022, emphasizes the importance of self-care as a transformative approach to improving health outcomes. Self-care interventions are recognized as critical tools for enhancing health systems and empowering individuals. These interventions are particularly relevant in addressing global health challenges, such as the anticipated shortage of 18 million health workers by 2030, the increasing demand for humanitarian assistance, and the ongoing threat of pandemics like COVID-19. Self-care interventions promote autonomy, self-efficacy, and active participation in health management. They are designed to be accessible, acceptable, and affordable, enabling individuals to take greater control of their health. These interventions are essential for advancing universal health coverage (UHC) and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 3, which focuses on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all. The guideline highlights the need for innovative strategies that extend beyond traditional health-sector responses. It underscores the importance of primary healthcare as a cornerstone for achieving UHC and emphasizes the role of self-care interventions in improving health outcomes, increasing access to services, reducing health disparities, and enhancing the quality of care. The WHO recommends self-care interventions as a means to empower individuals, families, and communities to optimize their health. These interventions include evidence-based tools such as high-quality drugs, devices, diagnostics, and digital solutions that can be used independently or with minimal support from health workers. The guideline also provides evidence-based recommendations and good practice statements to promote equitable access to self-care interventions, particularly for underserved populations and resource-limited settings. The conceptual framework for self-care interventions integrates people-centered and health systems approaches. It advocates for a holistic perspective that considers individual circumstances, needs, and preferences across the life course. A safe and supportive enabling environment is essential for the successful implementation and scale-up of self-care interventions, ensuring that they are accessible and appropriate for marginalized populations. In summary, the WHO guideline on self-care interventions serves as a comprehensive resource for advancing health and well-being through innovative, people-centered strategies. It provides a roadmap for integrating self-care into health systems, empowering individuals, and addressing global health challenges.
